subtopic: COMMEMORATION FUND FOR RESEARCH IN CHILDREN'S DISEASES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: ROYAL VISIT
subtopic: COMMEMORATION FUND FOR RESEARCH IN CHILDREN'S DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one week from today Her Majesty the Queen will once more set foot on Canadian soil. As Canadians prepare to welcome her, I think it is appropriate that I should make an announcement which I feel sure will be of general interest. The Queen has always shown a personal interest and concern in and devotion to the welfare and physical well-being of children; therefore in place of the usual presentation it has been considered desirable that the commemoration of her visit take the beneficiary form of a fund which would provide new hope for Canadian children.
This matter has been brought to her attention and she has been graciously pleased to approve the proposal of the Canadian government that a fund for research in children's diseases be established. With Her Majesty's consent the fund will be known as the Queen Elizabeth II fund for research in children's diseases.
The purpose of the fund will be to provide financial aid to institutions and individuals in Canada engaged in research in children's diseases, a field of medical science in which many problems remain unsolved.
The amount of the fund will be $1 million, for which amount the government will shortly ask parliament for its acceptance. I should add, too, that without in any way constituting a suggestion, much less a direction in this regard, if any provincial or municipal authorities desiring especially to mark the visit of Her Majesty would desire to do so, the Queen has signified that she would be happy if the fund were to be the beneficiary of any additional contributions which might be offered from such sources.
May I express satisfaction that it is possible, in thus commemorating her forthcoming visit, to manifest in her name as
Queen of Canada support for the efforts being pursued in all parts of the country toward the progressive elimination of the scourge of diseases affecting children.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ROYAL VISIT
subtopic: COMMEMORATION FUND FOR RESEARCH IN CHILDREN'S DISEASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will have heard with great pleasure the Prime Minister's announcement. In so far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we warmly support this proposal as a most imaginative and constructive way of commemorating Her Majesty's visit. If there could be additional contributions to the fund by provincial and municipal authorities and perhaps even by private individuals, that might make the fund even more important in carrying out the great work which the Prime Minister has mentioned.
I am quite certain that Her Majesty will get a great deal more satisfaction from this kind of gift than from another mink coat or piece of jewelry. I am also satisfied that Canadian children in the years to come, because of the work done through this fund commemorating her visit, may have cause to remember the visit with even greater joy than would ordinarily be the case.

maintopic: ROYAL VISIT
subtopic: COMMEMORATION FUND FOR RESEARCH IN CHILDREN'S DISEASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. group feel that the Prime Minister's announcement is most appropriate. We believe that Her Majesty and Canadian citizens generally will welcome and support the proposal to provide a million dollar fund for research into children's diseases as a most suitable indication of the esteem of Canadian citizens for Her Majesty. I am certain that Her Majesty will derive great personal satisfaction from this tribute in the realization that for many years to come the fund will be used to improve the lives and increase the hopes and happiness of certain of Her Majesty's subjects, those who are stricken in childhood, so their future may be brighter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening when the house adjourned I was discussing a matter which had already been introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, and that was the allimportant question, for a number of us, of the construction of the Champlain waterway or cut-off, as it is often called; or again, the deepening of the Richelieu.
I think I had almost completed my remarks, and I will not detain the house unduly, but there are one or two additional points I would like to make. However, before making them I think I should say this, that after the house adjourned one hon. member, with whom I am friendly, indicated to me that perhaps it would not be opportune to give consideration to this question when there is at the present time so much uncertainty about additional facilities at Welland. While I welcome that suggestion from the hon. member, which I think is very much to the point, it does seem to me, sir, that the two projects are not exclusive of each other.
Before I return to my original point I would like to pause here for a moment to remind the Minister of Transport that on an earlier occasion I asked him whether or not consideration was being given by the seaway authority engineers to the duplication of facilities at Welland. He avoided the question, as he sometimes does in his very elusive manner. But here may I make this suggestion to the minister. I said before that it is too early to determine now whether or not the facilities at Welland are sufficient. It would take at least one navigation season in order to determine that, if not two, but as the committee knows much of the work on the St. Lawrence seaway has been completed and many of the trusted officers and engineers have been forced to find work elsewhere.
Would it not be an excellent idea if some of those engineers who were associated with the special projects branch of the Department of Transport were retained in order to make a study of the cost and the economics of duplicating the single locks in the Welland canal? There is no doubt if that job were to be done it would take some years and would cost substantial sums of money. Therefore it seems to me to be opportune at this time for the special projects branch of the department to give consideration to that suggestion. I wonder whether the minister when he replies would not be so good as to let the

committee know whether this matter will be attended to, if it has not already been started.
I come back now to the question I was discussing in the first place. I do not think that by any stretch of the imagination these two projects are exclusive one of the other. On the contrary, I believe that if the Richelieu and Champlain cut-off were constructed it would add to the potential and increase the traffic of the St. Lawrence seaway. If I could pause here for a moment I should like to bring to the attention of the committee one of the findings of the international joint commission dealing with the Champlain waterway in April of 1937, concerning the costs.
After having come to the conclusion that five routes had been under discussion the commission stated that the estimated capital cost and annual carrying charges for the construction of a 12-foot waterway from the St. Lawrence to the Hudson via lake Champlain would be approximately $12,884,000 and $953,000 respectively; that the estimated annual cost and annual carrying charges for the construction of a 14-foot waterway would be approximately $50 million and $2,738,000 respectively, and that the estimated capital cost and annual carrying charges for the construction of a 27-foot waterway would be approximately $342,205,000 and $17,646,000 respectively. This will give the committee some idea of what was envisaged in 1937 by way of cost for the three depths of waterway, 12-foot, 14-foot and 27-foot.
My colleague the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres dealt with the technical aspects of the waterway from the United States side right up to the international border and then on up the St. Lawrence river. In the remarks I am making now I am not suggesting any route, because the commission in its report had under consideration five different routes and it may be that with the St. Lawrence seaway having been developed new routes not under consideration at that time should be considered today. I am certainly not in a position to say so. I believe that is a matter for a board of engineers. That is why I reiterate the statement I made last evening and on several previous occasions, that a board of engineers be established which would study the economics, the cost and the traffic aspects of this route.
I need not tell the committee that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys as well as the Minister of Defence Production, I believe, if not the Solicitor General as well, have received very strong representations in connection with this matter. I am sure their interest in this project is as keen as my own. I have not the slightest doubt that these three hon. gentleman have brought to the attention of the government the various aspects
Supply-Transport
of the problem. However, having had some experience in government I know that very often it is not possible for ministers to rise and say everything they would like to say on occasions such as this because of government policy concerning this and other matters affecting other parts of Canada. I am sure they will not disagree with me when I rise and put forward for the attention of the government the various aspects of this problem.
It seems to me that the time has arrived, as stated in the report of the international joint commission, for that commission to be seized de novo of the problem. I believe the international joint commission should be asked to consider it once again. It strikes me that because of the time limitation mentioned in the original report, in which it was stated that this matter should not be considered until after the St. Lawrence seaway had been completed, the time has now arrived for a study of it. It is not too much to ask the government to study it. It would not be a commitment. I think the people interested are entitled to know what are the economic, traffic and financial aspects of the problem, and the only way to do that is through the establishment of a board of engineers or the reference of the question to the international joint commission.
I am sure if the government were to do that it would be a step in the right direction. I need hardly say that I am delighted the Prime Minister is in his seat. I know he takes great interest in problems of national development, and this certainly is one which envisages both Canada and the United States. I ask him if he will not give the matter consideration in the light of the remarks I have just made.
There is one other matter I should like to discuss before I resume my seat. I have taken it up on other occasions, but to me it is a problem of great importance. As the committee knows, once the St. Lawrence seaway was completed a number of canals disappeared. The Soulanges canal disappeared-not physically, I hope, but it disappeared from a point of view of navigation-because the route is now moved from the northern part of lake St. Francis down through the Beauharnois canal. The Lachine canal does not disappear but will continue to service industry so long as industry remains there. The movement of the 27-foot draft ships will be up the south shore through the new locks at St. Lambert and Cote St. Catherine. As hon. members may be aware, several of the Ontario-St. Lawrence canals will disappear including the Farran's Point canal, the Rapide Plat canal, the Williamsburg canal, the Cornwall canal and the Iroquois canal. In fact they are gone now. They are under water save and except about

Supply-Transport
2\ to 3 miles of the Cornwall canal. With the disappearance of these canals-if not physically, as I have said, at least from the point of view of traffic-also go the employees, and that is the point I want to deal with. I ask, what will happen to the employees of these canals? I know the minister has the problem under consideration; I know the minister and his officers have given this problem pretty serious consideration. I know that in some cases they have succeeded in finding jobs which were adequate for people who have been displaced, which were equal to the jobs they had before; but I also know of a number of cases which I personally took up with the minister where that has not been possible, where that was not done. I am now asking the minister whether he will bring the committee up to date on the position of all these employees of the Department of Transport on the various canals. These employees have been there for many years, some of them I think for as long as 35 or 40 years, and others have been there a shorter length of time.
In answer to a question which I put on Hansard it was indicated to me what the position was at that time. I think it was indicated that in the eastern district, that is concerning the Lachine canal, there were about 230 employees affected. It was indicated that in the central district, which included the Soulanges and Beauharnois canals, there were 136 employees affected, and in the Ontario-St. Lawrence canals, the western district, there were 225 employees affected, making a total of 591. In the return I think it was indicated that it had been possible to find employment under the St. Lawrence authority for 432 of those employees, leaving 159 without work. I believe that was in April of this year, and I hope the position is better now than it was at that time.
So as not to rise again on the matter, 1 would like to bring certain things to the attention of the house. The minister may remember that on a similar occasion some years ago, in 1954 as a matter of fact, the Department of Transport disposed of certain assets in British Columbia to the British Columbia Telephone Company. These telephone services were operated by the Department of Transport. An agreement had been made with the British Columbia Telephone Company under which the employees of the Department of Transport would be taken on, and the officers of the Department of Transport did their best to make sure that no one would lose employment because of the transfer. They succeeded in large part but they did not succeed in full and when I came before the house with my estimates there was no one more insistent than the British

Columbia members that there should be no one who, having been an employee of the Department of Transport, should suffer because of the transfer and because of the exchange.
I was impelled by the strength of the argument to indicate to the officers of the department that I left a great deal more should be done than had already been done. I remind the committee that on that occasion more than one member said that the financial treatment because of the transfer was much better with the new corporation than with the Department of Transport, although certain superannuation benefits were perhaps not as good.
The result was that the Minister of Justice, then the member for Kamloops, as he still is, rose in the house and spoke at some length on the matter. After a full discussion of the whole matter by parliament, after parliament had been given the views not only of the member for Kamloops but also of a number of the members from the C.C.F. party, it was felt that no one should be left without employment because of that transfer.
I am happy to report that in the discussion which followed I think most members of the house felt that the arrangement made was satisfactory. I am not going so far as to say, sir, that no one was left without employment. No, that was not the case. I think I was able to report that, dealing with certain other employees of the Department of Transport who were displaced because of radio matters-260-odd members -employment had been found for every one of them with the exception of 7, and among those there was, of course, the difficulty of age.
I am sure the officers of the Department of Transport and the minister himself will want to see to it that no injustice is done in this case. May I go a step further and make this statement. I hope it will not be found to be an exaggerated one. I believe it is the responsibility of the Department of Transport to see that every one of those canal employees who has been displaced is given a job similar or closely similar to the one he had before. I know that is a difficult task. I know it is not easy when you move from one branch of government to another to meet that requirement. But I know the sympathetic attitude of those who are dealing with this problem. I am sure they will keep that in mind. I am as convinced now as I have always been that when, because of a great public project, a large body of men are displaced there is an obligation, certainly a moral and an equitable obligation,

on the part of the state to see to it that similar employment is given to the man who has been displaced.
I do not want to deal with individual cases; I have taken them up with the minister. He has been very courteous in his treatment of those individual cases, but there are a number of individual cases where the employment found is not nearly comparable to that which existed before. On behalf of all those employees I ask that consideration be given to the matter with the end in view of seeing that no one is left without employment.
I wonder whether the minister could bring me up to date on the present position.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I shall be very glad to. First of all, the hon. member for Laurier suggested that the St. Lawrence seaway authority keep a nucleus of engineering staff for future planning and operations. Several months ago the president of the St. Lawrence seaway authority spoke to me about this matter and made that suggestion to me. I readily agreed that this was desirable, and it has been in operation for some time now.
The hon. member mentioned what might be done to speed up operations in the Welland canal. That is under active study at the present time, and it would appear that the most effective thing we could do would be to introduce mooring walls between certain of the locks. It is estimated that this should increase the over-all capacity of the canal by about six ships per day.
The hon. member spoke about the Richelieu canal, and I should like to read him a short report made to me by the members of our economics division and the public works engineers who are working on this project at the present time. It reads as follows:
file previous cost estimates are now being revised in the light of recent alternative plans and present-day costs by the Department of Public Works, and when these are completed some estimate can be made of the volume of traffic required to justify improvements to the present canals and studies will be made to determine probable traffic available.

Before I sit down I want to finish the questions that were brought up yesterday. The hon. member for Vancouver East suggested yesterday that the return to address No. 67, calling for the production of correspondence, documents, etc. dealing with claims made by contractors for payments by the St. Lawrence seaway authority, was not complete, and to substantiate his remarks he produced and laid on the table an affidavit of Redmond Grant which referred to documents which the latter presented to me in December, 1958. Attached to the affidavit was what purports to be a record of the proceedings of a meeting of contractors discussing ways and means of presenting their claims to the government. These appendages to the affidavit are marked "confidential".
The matters which concerned me in connection with Mr. Grant's submission were complaints of faulty work in the construction of piers for the Cornwall island south channel bridge and in the painting of mitre gates. I did not concern myself with the "confidential" documents relating to contractors' claims. I did not know how they came into the possession of Mr. Grant or whether he was authorized to make them public. As I said some time earlier this session when the debate was taking place on the St. Lawrence seaway and when I was asked if I was aware of this report of contractors' meetings, I said I had

no knowledge of it and I did not. It is not a matter that I have any recollection of Mr. Grant having discussed with me when I met him in my office some time last fall.
Return No. 67 was, of course, compiled from the official records in the normal way. I reviewed the return before submission, and as far as I knew it represented a proper and complete return in the terms of the address. Any references to contractors' claims in the submission made to me by Mr. Grant were incidental and confidential, and the propriety of including these documents in the return was certainly questionable. As I have said, the matters complained of by Mr. Grant which concerned me were his suggestions of improper workmanship by seaway contractors.
As to the Cornwall island south channel bridge, I was very familiar with that matter and followed closely the remedial measures required. In answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver East, complete details were furnished and I shall repeat the gist of the information then given:
The Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Limited was retained by the seaway authority to review all field information, the decisions made and the procedures followed in the construction of the piers, and to give an opinion as to the adequacy of remedial measures undertaken. A preliminary report, dated January 11, 1958, included a statement that ". . . and the remedial measures being taken are reasonable ones".
In view of the concern subsequently expressed in some quarters as to the adequacy of the piers, the corps of engineers, United States army and the seaway authority appointed an independent board of consultants to investigate and to rule or recommend on the matter. This board comprised Emil H. Praeger of Praeger-Kavanagh, consulting engineers, New York; G. F. Ferris, president of Raymond International Inc.; and D. F. Murphy, chief structural engineer of Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Limited.
The board first met on April 4, 1958, when it approved of the remedial measures adopted. Following a thorough investigation of all features of work performed, the board, in its final report dated October 14, 1958, stated that the piers and the soil on which they rest are now adequate to safely sustain all dead and maximum live loads.
As to Mr. Grant's complaint concerning the painting of mitre gates, the president of the seaway authority reported to me as follows:
There has been a suggestion that unsatisfactory work was accepted in connection with the painting of certain lock gates, as reported upon by the War-nock Hersey Company Limited, who were employed as inspectors. Certain objectionable features were observed and remedial measures were taken, or are to be taken, to restore the vinyl system of painting to an acceptable condition. The chief engineer of the St. Lawrence seaway authority has reported as follows:
"Although, as indicated by the inspection company, the surface texture and appearance of the painting does not strictly comply with the requirements of the specifications, this can be observed only by close examination and will certainly not be apparent when the gates are placed in service.

"The important feature is that, despite the somewhat uneven surface, the paint has been applied to at least the minimum specified thickness and its adhesive properties are excellent. It is expected that the durability of the paint will be as great as that contemplated.
"Some of the walkways, handrail and diagonals had been shop painted without first having received a wash coat, with the result that there was improper adhesion. These parts were recleaned and completely repainted to specified requirements.
"The authority may be assured that neither the Warnock Hersey Company nor the authority engineers will accept workmanship inferior to the specified, except for the somewhat rough surface texture in some areas which are of insignificant importance."
It is the practice of the authority to retain sufficient security to ensure proper completion of the work.
The house may be interested in the status of Mr. Grant, who issued the affidavit. He was employed by the seaway authority in their inspection branch in May, 1957 at $300 a month. He resigned in March, 1958 when his salary was $310 a month, giving poor health as the reason for his resignation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East and perhaps also the hon. member for Assiniboia appear to be concerned by reason of the representations they have received from Mr. Grant, and perhaps others, concerning faulty work by contractors on seaway construction. I know there have been difficulties, arising partly from the urgency of having to complete the work on schedule. On the other hand there is a danger in exaggerating the situation and leaving an improper impression on the public. I make the suggestion that I would be very glad, at any time that would suit the convenience of the hon. members for Assiniboia and Vancouver East, to arrange a meeting at Ottawa at which the responsible officials of the seaway authority would discuss with them the complaints they have received, and indicate to them the action which has been taken by the authority. I would be very glad to arrange such a meeting, and to see that all relevant documents are made available to them.

I would like to make a reference to the minister, since I am speaking for the first time on his estimates. About a year ago I was travelling west by train and I was in company, fortunately I will say, with a number of young Progressive Conservatives who were returning from a gathering in the east. They began discussing the future of the party, and they were in almost unanimous agreement that the Minister of Transport was going to be the crown prince or was the crown prince of the party. I was telling them I thought they should wait a bit and see how the crown prince performed with this particular department before they went overboard.
Supply-Transport
In so far as his performance in this department is concerned, and it is one I have followed more closely than any other in the House of Commons, it has not been one that has impressed me very much.
I have a strong impression that the deputy minister has too much work to do and that there needs to be one or two more deputy ministers in the department. I hope when the parliamentary assistants are handed out this department will get a couple of them, because I think the very situation that developed in connection with the Malton land deal is an indication that perhaps there should be a bit closer rapport between the elected assembly and the officials of this department.
The Malton case interested me many months ago. I put a question on the order paper which, unfortunately, could not be answered because a decision had not yet been rendered by the court. I have no question or doubt about the integrity or honesty of the hon. member for Peel. In many ways I admire the stand he tried to take throughout the whole situation, but the problem brings up the whole question of the functions of a member of parliament. The hon. member for Peel had some constituents with a very definite grievance. This grievance was turned down in a court of law, in effect, but long before that he brought it to the attention of the minister. According to the evidence he gave he got some kind of undertaking from the minister, in the presence of some of the minister's officials, as to what would be done. Unfortunately the minister could not follow up on the undertaking to the hon. member for Peel, and we have to accept the fact that there is confusion as to just what was said or just what was accepted at that particular meeting.
In my opinion this particular case has significance because one often hears that opposition members are ineffective and, in a sense, are just futile mouthers of words; that one needs to be a government member in order to get anything done. This seems to be a case where a government member, a member with a strong enough personality and ability to be appointed whip of the party, was not able to achieve his particular goal. In a sense I almost regret it, because I think in this particular case he had some real worth and some real justice behind his request.
What does a member of parliament do when he has a constituent problem such as this, and he gets some kind of undertaking from the minister or from the officials to investigate the matter? There seems to be a kind of no man's land in here in which the position of the member of parliament is

Supply-Transport
extremely indefinite. I do not know whether it could be or should be defined, but certainly I think this is one demonstration of the lack of power and the lack of influence of the member of parliament. I am not speaking particularly of the member of parliament for Peel. I think this is an indicator, in a general way, for all members of parliament.
We are continually getting requests from our constituencies: would we try to do something about a certain situation, a personal grievance or a regional area grievance. We take it up with the officials and the minister and in some cases we get attention, while in other cases we get the brush-off. The Department of Transport seems to be one of those in which we get the brush-off more often than we get attention, but certainly it is not as bad as the Department of National Defence or some of the others.
In this particular kind of case, what position has the member of parliament in so far as his word is concerned? What undertaking could we have? It seems to me one of the faults in this case is that we do not have any kind of written account as to what took place at this particular meeting. I first became interested in this case when it was brought up in the Telegram by one of the columnists. The position she took was harshly critical of the minister. I was attracted by her phrase that these people had been "Heesed out". Later another correspondent for the same paper, Mr. Peter Dempson, wrote a long story which appeared on November 14 and November 15 of last year, trying to present the matter from the minister's point of view.
I cannot make out from this, or from the story given to the house, what is the minister's conception of the position of a member of parliament, and I would suggest that in future dealings with all members of parliament he should try to put something on record so we shall not misunderstand what the minister wants, or means because I am confident that the hon. member for Peel did not realize that the minister did not have the authority to give him an assurance.
In closing my remarks on this subject I should like to reiterate that there is no question at all in my mind about the integrity of the hon. member for Peel. I think he was honest and direct throughout the whole course of these events, but we are still left in the position that the individual member of parliament, whether supporting the government or the opposition, has a very peculiar relationship and a very indefinite relationship to many of the purposes he is seeking to achieve. My own comment on that is that anything we can do to increase, I will not say the power but certainly the scope and the ability of a member of parliament to

perform a more important function than he is performing at the present time should be under consideration at all times by the government and the house.
The next point I wish to raise in dealing with these estimates arises from a great deal of contact which I have had in the last ten days or so with people who work with the Canadian National Railway and who are interested in the Canadian National Railway, and I wish to bring this up in fairness to the president of that railway, Mr. Donald Gordon. Following the meetings this session of the standing committee on railways, the impression has gone widely abroad that Mr. Gordon treated members of that committee in a rough, tough and nasty fashion and that he, in a phrase, put the members of parliament in their place.
Mr. Chairman, I attended every meeting of that committee and I did not get that impression, though it is certainly the impression that is abroad in the country. In consequence, many employees of the C.N.R. who have always doubted Mr. Gordon's knowledge of railway problems have been incensed about this and have said, "What are you members of parliament going to do about the president telling you off?" To be fair to Mr. Gordon, he made his remarks on the functions of the committee after he had been persistently asked by me to make his comments on the work of that body.
I have been on the committee for two years and I have gone back over its records in previous years, and I am as willing as any other member of the committee to admit that its performance could be improved. That is why I wanted to get suggestions from the president as to what he thought about the ways in which the committee could be improved. I was disappointed that the committee did not bring to the house any of the recommendations which Mr. Gordon said he would give us. It seems to me that we could take a better look, in committee, at the operations of the Canadian National railroad; but I want to put it clearly on record, as perhaps the most persistent questioner in the committee, that I had no feeling at any time that Mr. Gordon had told us off. As far as I am concerned he only gave us information which he was asked to give. My only regret is that somehow that committee did not function well enough to enable us to enquire more deeply and in a more informed manner into the operations of the railway.
I cannot resist making some remarks about lakehead harbour and shipping, and, in particular, the lakehead harbour commission. We have had a provincial election campaign going on, and right at the centre of it in.

our region has been the lakehead harbour commission. I remember telling the minister months ago that if the government is going to appoint Conservatives to this commission it should remember that there are smart Conservatives and some Conservatives who are not so smart, and I appealed to him to appoint some smart Conservatives.
We put through the bill setting up the lake-head harbour commission last August. The commission held its first meeting only about three weeks ago. All that delay, coupled with the fact that an expert from the Department of Transport did not reach the lake-head until May 18 to consult with the local people, is an indication to me of the correctness of my remarks on an earlier occasion about the way this department operates. I have a very definite feeling-and this is one of the concrete examples-that the burden of work is too heavy on the senior men in this department. Otherwise how can one explain that a commission which is given authority to get moving last August does not hold its first meeting until May 18, after the first foreign ships are through the seaway?
In a political sense this has not redounded to the credit of the Progressive Conservatives either federally or provincially, but that is aside from the point. We need a lakehead harbour commission which has members with a great deal of initiative and background, people who will work hard and really set up something which will make our lakehead one of the best ports on the lakes. But if the performance of this commission up to now is an example, it shows that there is a sad future ahead.
One of the things in connection with this commission which has bothered me is the fact that several of its members are definitely employees of interested parties. I raised this point with the minister before and he decided not to make it an issue, but the fact remains that the C.N.R. owns a great deal of property in the harbour, while Canada Steamship Lines has a very active business into the harbour and also owns a shipyard there. Yet employees of both the Canadian National Railways and of the Canada Steamship Lines are members of the commission. These two employees happen to have been appointed by two cities; they are appointed members. That, of course, is the responsibility of the cities. Evidently the minister did not feel that he could or should check that. But the other three members are chosen by the minister, and I should like to ask the minister if he could explain how he came to make these particular choices. I should also like him to explain the relationship of his government to
Supply-Transport
the provincial government with regard to the provision of transport facilities out of the lakehead harbour in this interim period before the terminal is completed.
One of the most enjoyable things about the election campaign is that it brought Premier Frost into our area on two occasions, and on each occasion he made the point that he was a partner with the federal government in this magnificent lakehead harbour development and all that was going to follow from it.
We are still left with the situation that between the Manitoba border and the lake-head we have no decent road as far as any kind of heavy traffic is concerned, and I should appreciate it very much if the minister would explain to me what conversations he has had with the provincial authorities about the provision of proper routes out of the lakehead harbour.
There is very definite concern in our particular region over the Welland canal toll structure, and a very definite feeling that the government should consider whether it would be possible to abandon these tolls at the end of this shipping season. I know there is a feeling which extends very widely in western Canada, judging by newspaper reports that such a step should be taken, and I know this feeling is also very strong in the Hamilton and St. Catharines regions. I hope this is something which the minister will have his experts consider.
One of the points which come up many times along the lakes is the whole question of shipbuilding. I have often wondered whether some of the present cabinet ministers have not given their speeches of a few years ago to the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. member has been making speeches around the country, including one at the lake-head, about the need for Canada to have both a salt water and a fresh water fleet. This is very much along the old line taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and some of the other members of the cabinet, including the present Minister of Transport.
We have had indications that the shipbuilding industry along the lakes is in for pretty heavy weather, specifically at the lake-head, and I would like to ask the minister if at some time during the discussion of his estimates he would review the shipbuilding situation and the prospects for the shipyards along the great lakes. I know there is very definite confusion at the lakehead as to our inability to obtain any substantial contracts. The issue is confused, and in view of the fact that the shipyards are a subsidiary of a

Supply-Transport
much larger concern, in effect Canada Steamship Lines, I would very much appreciate it if the minister could give us an outline in this particular field.
One of the questions I would like to ask the minister, which could be answered when we are dealing specifically with the radio regulations, and I want to give him notice of it, is whether it is still impossible for anyone to get a radiotelephone in his car if he is not a British subject or a Canadian citizen; that is, as an individual. If this is so I would like an explanation in that regard. I would also like from the minister later on an explanation as to when his department is going to abbreviate its regulations and make it easier for a model enthusiast to use radio frequencies in controlling various models which he may use in his hobby. If the minister would give me that information later it would be very much appreciated.

Certainly. Albert Sabourin and Ivan Castonguay.
Moreover, since the change of administration, about 60 of the 130 permanent and temporary employees of the Soulanges canal have been transferred to the seaway, while 20 or 30 kept their work at Soulanges, and several others were transferred to Lachine. Those men could be asked about the guarantee that was offered them by the Liberal party under the former administration and about the security they are now enjoying thanks to the present administration.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I heard the former president of the seaway complain and express his disappointment about the bad publicity received by the seaway late last season, when a great many ships were icebound in the Lachine canal and in Montreal harbour as a result of sudden very cold weather and an early fall.
Contrary to the statements of the hon. former member for Stormont-now member for Laurier, by grace of importation-I hold excellent publicity was given that misadventure in Montreal harbour. Every day-[DOT] not to say every hour-radio, TV and all newspapers reported the progress made now by nature, now by the icebreakers, or again by canals or Montreal harbour employees. To prove this, I would say that, as soon as the seaway was opened this year, as soon as it was ice free, so many large freighters sailed into the waterway that there was a bottleneck at the entrance. This proves that, if there really was some bad publicity last fall, shipowners refused to believe it. Anyhow, it was not as unfavourable as the hon. gentleman from Cornwall would have us believe by making statements which have no basis whatever on facts.
I wonder why our hon. friend should have done this? Is it to distort the facts? It is a well known and widely used Liberal practice to sow doubt in people's minds, to make equivocal statements, and to lie in thought as well as in words, wilfully and with impunity.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday we heard the hon. member for Laurier demand a public statement by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) about a so-called contradiction referred to by the president of the Court of the Exchequer. I wonder whether he himself could not make a statement on professional ethics because one day, at the time when my hon. friend was president of the seaway- around 1956-a professional engineer working for the seaway authority was denied the right to leave his job-by the then president, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier-to take another job with the Miron Manibeque Company, a firm which then had contracts with the seaway. My good friend, sometime president of the seaway, argued that professional ethics did not allow a professional engineer working for the seaway authority to quit his job and take on another one with a contractor working under that same authority.
Now, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend, who professes sacred respect for professional ethics is now a member of the legal firm Geoffrion and Prud'homme, lawyers for the Canit-Canamont company which has now claims against the seaway authority. In other words, the former president of the seaway, who laboured from 1954 to 57 to see this great scheme carried through, and who necessarily is privy to all its secrets, is now preparing to tear down part of his handiwork on behalf of a few contractors who happen to be his friends. If this can be described as professional ethics, it surely needs a genuinely Liberal mind to see it in that light.
After I am through with my remarks, I should like to hear my good friend make a statement on professional ethics, instead of calling for such a statement from the present Minister of Transport.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member (I mean the former member from Cornwall) referred to the popularity of the seaway. He should have consulted the railway companies, the manufacturers of rolling stock, railway employees, canal employees, and people in Montreal, Lachine, Vaudreuil, Soulanges and Cornwall, before making statements on the popularity of the seaway. I am not saying that the seaway should not have been built, but this is a far cry from saying it is popular. Perhaps it is popular with the shipping companies and a few others, 66968-9-290
S upp ly-Transport
but I would point out that one of its drawbacks, one of the main obnoxious features lies in the fact that railway companies stand to lose plenty because of it.
The cost of railway operations in that area is bound to go up. That is partly the reason why the railways, both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., are planning to hike their passenger rates 17 to 37 per cent. Recently, under pressures from every municipality in the district from Montreal to Rigaud, the board of transport commissioners held hearings in Montreal and all the parties concerned were able to express their views.
If those increases are authorized, several of those municipalities will be quite seriously affected. The municipalities of Pointe Claire, Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Dorion, Comeau, Hudson and Rigaud, especially the last four, many of whose people commute by rail to their jobs in Montreal, will find their future development greatly jeopardized unless other steps are taken to make it less expensive for those people to travel to and from work.
If it were proven that the railway companies are operating their commuter service at a loss, I would support any measure designed to maintain the present level of rates.
Since large amounts of money were spent for research on war equipment which proved unnecessary, manufacturers of rolling stock could also be subsidized, but for much more human and permanent reasons.
Practically all our passenger cars and diesel locomotives are of entirely American design. I feel it would be in everyone's interest if certain research was undertaken to produce passenger cars of purely Canadian design which would be much more economical and, at the same time, more comfortable for commuters.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the attention of the house to some of the arguments put forward by the municipalities in their submission to the board of transport commissioners, in an effort to avoid an increase in commuter rates.
Unquestionably one of the most interesting resolutions was the one prepared by the municipality of lie Perrot, part of which reads as follows:
Whereas, since the last rate increase, the service has been cut down instead of being improved,
Whereas a rate increase can only be an economic burden for the present users of the regular service;

Whereas, on economic grounds too, the rate increase will fail of its purpose by cutting down the number of train users.
Whereas any increase is likely to jeopardize the demographic expansion of our region;
Whereas the municipalities' power of taxation over railways is limited;
Whereas the service to employees has been curtailed and that, in the interest of commuters, the service should be improved, and no existing train should be changed or eliminated;

Mr. Chairman, those are some of the reasons set forth by the municipality of lie Perrot.

Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed on this item to point out through you to the Minister of Transport a matter which was raised last year at the same time by my colleague the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets).
At first sight the matter seems to be of a local nature, since it affects particularly the people of Hochelaga and Maisonneuve-Rose-mont counties.
On second thought however, if one takes time to consider the relations existing between the general and local interests, a question of principle is involved that cannot be evaded or made light of.
I am referring to the railroad tracks which run from Moreau street, cut through Hochelaga, Maisonneauve-Rosemont and Mercier counties, along the St. Lawrence river, and toward the north-east of Montreal island right up to the end of the island. Built in 1913 by the Canadian Northern Quebec Railways Company, those tracks have since then been taken over by the Canadian National Railways.
Although, unquestionably they have considerably hindered the commercial expansion and housing development in Hochelaga and Maisonneuve-Rosemont counties, those railway tracks were for some years very useful and even essential. For instance, three passenger trains, including one that went as far as Chicoutimi, used those tracks daily in both directions. The tracks were also used by many east or westbound freight trains on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river.
That was in another era. In 1913, the section of the Montreal island crossed by those tracks in Hochelaga and Maisonneuve coun-
Supply-Transport
ties, was almost entirely comprised in the town of Maisonneuve which has since been annexed to the city of Montreal.
At the time, that section of the island had a population of a few thousand.
Those tracks were then running across vacant lots, intersected by a few sparsely built streets.
Today the population there is well above
200,000.
If we consider this population on the basis of the area it occupies, we surely arrive at one of the highest ratios of population density in Canada.
This increase in population, and the general progress, have wrought a complete change in the make-up and the topography of this Montreal area.
Since the central station was built, the Moreau station was torn down. High-level railways were built in the north-western district on Montreal island. New streets were opened up. Numerous public buildings and thousands of new housing units were erected.
Passenger trains which used to stop at the Moreau station come now to the central station.
Except in rare cases, freight trains are now using these new high-level railways which were built further north on Montreal island.
However, these tracks are still there to serve, between Moreau and Viau streets, less than a score of rather averaged-sized plants, about eight of which are located in the Hochelaga riding. They are also used daily to carry a tank car train from the oil refineries in eastern Montreal. Near Moreau street, in Hochelaga, those cars transfer from C.N.R. to C.P.R. tracks.
Such today, on the basis of their necessity fifteen years ago, is the relatively negligible purpose served by those railroad tracks.
Besides, this "usefulness" factor is of very minor importance.
Indeed, the presence of those tracks gives rise to a problem which involves a much more important factor, the human factor. The mere study of the route followed by those rail tracks immediately reveals the implication of the human factor.
Starting in the neighbourhood of Moreau street, the tracks run eastward, along a line following Lafontaine street, across Ontario street and then along Rouen street.

Supply-Transport
Between Moreau and Viau streets, they cross more than 25 streets, which means that many level crossings.
Those 25 streets are situated on the island of Montreal, where the residential population attains one of the highest percentages of density.
From Notre Dame street, which runs along the busy commercial wharves of eastern Montreal, those streets are used not only by the local population but also for the daily transport of thousands of motor vehicles from all parts of the metropolitan area.
I am thinking more particularly of Pius IX boulevard, one of the most congested arteries of Montreal which crosses the entire island of Montreal between Pius IX wharf and the Prairie river bridge.
I also have in mind Ontario street, which is crossed by those tracks at the Valois intersection.
Ontario street is one of the largest commercial thoroughfares of Montreal. From both sides, and particularly in the ridings of Hoche-laga and Maisonneuve-Rosemont, Ontario street is bordered by shops representing invested capital of several million dollars. Public transportation buses constantly use that thoroughfare, with their large loads of passengers travelling to or from the centre of the metropolis or other large thoroughfares that cross the city.
On Ontario street, as on Pius the IX boulevard, and all other streets crossed by railway tracks, the traffic and movement of the population are particularly intense in the early morning and in the late afternoon.
At those hours workers and school children are travelling to or from work or school.
Let me point out that, between Moreau and Viau streets, some twenty schools and convents, about ten churches and eleven playgrounds are situated in the vicinity of the tracks.
Therefore, several times a day, thousands of citizens, walking or riding, have to cross the tracks either to go to some of those public buildings or to reach main perpendicular streets or thoroughfares such as St. Catherine, Adam, Lafontaine and Ontario.
Now it is generally during that period of the day when that heavy traffic of people and motor vehicles is at its peak that this train of tankers or other freight trains, happen to block one after the other, all streets between Viau and Moreau.

Ensuing delays and inconveniences can readily be realized.
That undesirable situation reaches its peak in the neighbourhood of Moreau street, where shunting of cars takes place between our two big railway companies.
Over an area which frequently covers six or seven streets eastward from Moreau street, the coming and going of those cars paralyse the traffic for periods of as much as half an hour at times, in flagrant and repeated violation of article 314, chapter 234 of the Railway Act, which limits such obstruction periods to five minutes.
At the corner of Prefontaine street, I personally have seen fire department vehicles immobilized at the crossings and having to wait there for more than fifteen minutes on account of that shunting of cars.
When that violation was later brought to the attention of the C.N.R. authorities, a member of the legal department of that company replied, very seriously, that in such circumstances, the vehicles had only to use some other street. As if it were possible to have those huge trucks back up and turn around in narrow streets, crowded over a distance of 100 feet with other vehicles that cannot move for the same reason!
It seems to me hardly necessary to describe the serious inconveniences as well as the numerous and grave prejudices which those railway crossings cause to the 200,000 persons who live in the constituencies of Hochelaga and Maisonneuve-Rosemont.
Those twenty-five railway crossings, or thereabouts, present a constant danger, especially to the thousands of children who live nearby or who, of necessity, have to cross them. For reasons of economy, I presume, the traditional gate guards have given way to signal lights which constitute a very weak means of defence against the mortal dangers that can be caused by the passage of a train across a densely populated street.
Finally, from the aesthetic point of view, those tracks are a disgrace which should no longer be countenanced in an era when town planning strives and manages, even in industrial areas, to introduce constructions and arrangements pleasing to the eye. The very presence of the tracks is, no doubt to a large extent, the reason for the considerable delay in developing that part of Montreal east, as compared to the west end of the metropolis.
Since 1951 the association of businessmen of eastern Montreal has repeatedly and urgently requested that those tracks be left unused, or removed. Practical and positive solutions were submitted to the authorities concerned, by that association. From Viau

street the westbound tank-cars could use the national harbours board trackage. Car shunting could then be made without obstructing traffic.
It must also be pointed out that the few plants served by the branch line extending from Viau street to Moreau street use their privilege only from time to time.
They might more easily, and probably at a saving, receive or ship their goods through other means, for instance by trucks travelling between those plants and the railway lines along the Montreal waterfront.
The C.N.R. legal division, taking a practical down-to-earth point of view, has replied to the association of businessmen of eastern Montreal that its recommendations and suggestions could not be considered.
Of course, the suggested relocation of these tracks would involve some expense for the railways but this would be of a very minor character, and the loss of revenue would be negligible.
That is precisely the problem. Must we allow a railroad company and perhaps 20 industrial firms to go on enjoying privileges which are neither essential nor necessary, to the detriment of the rights of over 200,000 people who pay exactly the same taxes as their fellow citizens who do not have to put up with the many serious problems arising from the presence and use of these tracks.
I should be grateful to the Minister of Transport if he would kindly look into this problem and get in touch with the C.N.R. authorities in order that the decision taken in this regard be seriously reconsidered, in the light of the broad principle as to whether individual interest should take precedence over public welfare.
