speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
If it does, I am sorry; nevertheless I think the minister should, as he has done, do his utmost to give us the facts so that, as the Leader of the Opposition said earlier, we will then be able to determine what our course of action should be. The minister put on the record today copies of the correspondence. I, of course, have not had the opportunity to read it all but I did read one letter, and I should like to put the second last paragraph on the record. Perhaps I should put the whole letter on the record. It is dated at Ottawa, October 24, 1957, addressed to the minister, and reads as follows:

Dear George:
Re: Malton airport expropriations
I hate to bother you with such things, but I have had a telephone call and a telegram; Bill Beach has had telephone calls; and apparently Speers, the land agent in Toronto, has made the statement that he and not the minister is running the department in Toronto.
I take it that Speers is the district appraiser of the Department of Transport in Toronto.
I have had a talk with Earl Clare, whom you appointed for the purpose of evaluating small holdings, and he tells me that Speers was in Ottawa today, apparently with some proposal to the deputy minister or assistant deputy minister that Clare be taken off the job.
Clare has already promoted the public relations of the Department of Transport more than the land agents have done in the last three and a half years. He has taken the time to examine each house and sit down and talk over the valuations which the owners want, with each owner. Needless to say, he will come to his own valuation.
Now I come to the second last paragraph.
I have known Clare for many, many years and he is not going to be influenced by Speers or any home owners. You may or may not hear of this through your deputies but, if so, I suggest that they be told in no uncertain terms that Speers is to get off Clare's back and let him do the valuations in his own way; if not, it defeats the purpose of appointing him.
No answer is expected and this, I suggest, might be ripped up and thrown away.
Well, I am not surprised that the last paragraph is in the letter, but in view of the second last paragraph I ask the minister this question. The minister has said here is a man who is so anxious to assist his constituents and do the very best he can to get a good deal for the small people, does the minister now think the sentiments contained in that second last paragraph are the kind of sentiments that should be expressed in the light of what has been discussed this afternoon, and does he think this is good administration on the part of a member of parliament?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Peel was only anxious to see that these valuations should be fair valuations, and in expressing that opinion he was only saying that in his opinion that was the way to see that the valuator, Mr. Clare, could carry out a fair and independent valuation which would get a square deal for the people whom the member for Peel represents in parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
The point is that the valuation was to be increased substantially and if one reads the judgment, which is quite clear in that respect, it leads one to believe that the moment these valuations were accepted then the 180 other cases would also have to be reopened. Whether or not they were adequate valuations I am not saying at the moment.
Sup p ly-Transport

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member where there is any support for that conclusion in the judgment? I have the judgment before me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Oh, there is no support for that in the judgment at all.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Now, just a moment. The Prime Minister asked me a fair question and I answered it frankly. Of course there is no suggestion of that in the judgment. It was not being considered. But I am making the point now that the moment you increase the valuations on 11 properties, how on earth are you going to leave the properties of 180 other people living alongside in the same district without increasing their valuations? It just cannot be done. I know that similar cases have taken place before-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Will the hon. member mention any cases-he will know, of course, because he was minister of transport-where final settlement had been made and thereafter as a result of court proceedings some adjoining property was valued at a higher amount Which required the reopening of the other cases? He said he knows of cases.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I took it that way.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister interrupted me before I finished my sentence.
What I was going to say was this: I know of cases in the Department of Transport where valuations having been made and a series of claims having been disposed of and the compensation money paid, adjacent owners came along and said, "We are not going to accept that valuation". Then, pressures were brought about, not only by groups but by municipalities, associations and even members of parliament who said, "We do not believe that valuation is a fair and reasonable one; we think it should be increased because of increased prices in the area, because industry may since have been located in the area," or because of other reasons of which I am not reminded at the moment. But we took the position at the time that it is up to the exchequer court to determine what the compensation was, and the moment the exchequer court determined what the valuation was, then that made the position quite clear in so far as the other expropriatees were concerned.
I come back to the statement I made earlier that while there is no mention in the judgment of the 180 other persons, the moment this valuation was accepted, the moment this agreement was made as was suggested and as was said in the judgment, then the

Supply-Transport
other 180 cases would, of necessity, have to be opened. This being the case, then the federal treasury is in a pretty serious position in so far as these people are concerned because 1 am sure the Department of Transport or the government would not want to treat a group of expropriatees in one part of an area in one manner by paying them one price, and another group just alongside differently by paying another price.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
If I may answer that, I would say that you have a distinct group of 180 people who were satisfied, who had signed with the department and whose deals were complete. So far as we know, they are quite satisfied. You had one small group of 12 people who said that they were not satisfied and it is, in a free country like this, your right to be either satisfied or not satisfied with the deal that is offered. These people said they were not. The hon. member for Peel felt that they had a good case and he decided to try to get them a square deal, to get them a fair valuation. That is all he tried to do.
I should like to ask the hon. member this. If in his riding there were a group of people who were satisfied with a certain valuation and a small group who were not, would he then say to them, "Oh, no, you have got to take what you are offered because 180 other people have been quite satisfied; I cannot go to the government because if you have been done a grievous wrong and if we look into it and find you have been done a grievous wrong we could not pay you any more because this would mean opening up a lot of other cases and that would cost the government a lot of money." If the hon. member were representing 12 constituents who felt they had a raw deal, would he not go to the government and fight tooth and nail to get them what he considered to be a square deal? Would he or would he not do that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I have no objection to my hon. friend's interruptions or his questions.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: This is a free and open debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Yes, certainly. He states that the group expropriated earlier, the 180, were satisfied with their valuation.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: As I understand it; they would not have signed if they were not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I accept that statement, but does the minister think for one moment the man next door who noticed the increase in valuation would be satisfied? Does he think for one moment that as soon as a neighbour gets an increase of $5,000 or $10,000 for his property, the man who settled before will not come back and ask for a similar increase?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I will answer that right now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Just a moment; that is what took place in a number of cases in the Department of Transport. All you need to do is consult your own officers in connection with expropriations.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I will answer that right now. In other words, if you have 20 constituents and 19 of them feel they have had a square deal but the 20th feels he has not-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: You have had six valuations already.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Just a minute; would the hon. member say, "I will not try to have your case opened up because if I do try, and even if I feel you had a raw deal, it would mean that the government would have to open up the other 19 cases and give them a similar deal." If that is the hon. member's attitude, then he will not be back next time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
The Chair has allowed the debate to continue for the last half-hour, but for the sake of relevancy I think it is about time we examined the situation. The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Laurier have both said that no attempt has been made to smear the hon. member for Peel or any other member, and the Chair is ready to believe that no such attempt was actually made.
However, these repetitious questions and repetitious answers have continued and it seems that the present basis of this debate is a hypothetical question as to whether or not, if this valuation had gone through, 180 individuals would have protested the former valuation to which they had agreed. It is impossible to expect a debate to be continued on such a hypothetical basis. I regret to say that unless hon. members of the opposition explain clearly the purpose of all these questions and answers, and the reason for this debate I shall have to declare this debate out of order because it is not relevant to the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if you so declare then there will be no doubt about the position which we, on this side of the house, will take. We will accept the ruling of the Chair, but I tell you in all honesty and in all sincerity, that I do not believe that would be an equitable decision. However, it will be up to you to determine, sir.
I do not want to pursue the matter unduly, but I am not going to let the Minister of Transport get away with the last statement he made, that if I continue asking these questions I will find myself without a seat.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I said, if that was your attitude toward your constituents you would not be back. I asked you a question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: My hon. friend need not worry too much about what is likely to happen in my constituency because-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: That is what George Marler said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
But my hon. friend's colleagues on the other side have done their best on two occasions not only to defeat me but to see that I would no longer be a member. They have not been successful. I do not imagine, judging by the popularity of the present government in the province of Quebec now, that they will be successful in the next election.
There are one or two questions I should like to ask the minister. Before I do, I should like him to comment on this particular part of the judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson, at page 16:
I have no hesitation in rejecting Mr. Clare's valuation. I do not believe that he was a free and independent appraiser. He admitted that Mr. Pallett, who had recommended his appointment, said that he wanted a good price and on his crossexamination, after long hesitation, he admitted that Mr. Pallett had instructed him to put as generous a valuation as possible on the properties and he told Mr. Speer, the Department of Transport's agent, that it was difficult for him to carry out his instructions.
Would the minister care to comment on that paragraph?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: As I have said to the hon. member several times, and as he knows, being a distinguished barrister, it is completely wrong to ask me to comment on a judgment which has been rendered.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: That is not true, of course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: That is so if the case were sub judice, but it is not. It is a judgment, and so far as I know it is not under appeal.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: It is still within the period within which an appeal could be taken.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
That does not make it sub judice; it becomes sub judice the moment the appeal is launched. An appeal not having been launched, it is proper for anyone to comment on it and therefore it is proper for the Minister of Transport to comment on it, but every time I ask him questions concerning the judgment he always comes back and says in his very breezy and easy manner: you should know better, you are a lawyer, and so forth. But that is not an answer to the question. Either the minister answers the question or he does not. If he
Supply-Transport
does not answer it, then that is fine. We accept that. If he chooses to answer it, that is another matter again.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I have answered every question which the hon. gentleman has put to me. He asked for material, and I have given it to him. This morning he asked for correspondence and I gave him far more than was necessary. I gave him all the letters that could be found.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: What do you mean by "far more than was necessary"?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I think it is completely wrong to ask a member of parliament to comment on a judgment of a presiding judge and I do not intend to do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: All right, I will leave it at that. I think the hon. gentleman is in error, but he is entitled to his opinion just as much as I am to mine.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: It is the only time I have refused.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Now I should like to ask the minister this: what is the position of the department with reference to the ten other cases which have not been disposed of?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: We have offered, I am advised, immediate settlement at valuations comparable to that in the judgment.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Is it not the intention of the minister, then, to give these other cases the benefit of the judgment of an independent valuator.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I am abiding, as I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would, by the judgment of the court.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am speaking for this group. We have listened very carefully to the discussion of this matter and we want to be very fair about it. First of all, let me say that we think it is most unfortunate that the hon. member for Peel is not in his seat while the estimates of the Minister of Transport are being discussed. It seems to us that everyone should have realized that this matter would have been brought to the attention of the committee.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but having read in the press of the intention of the Leader of the Opposition to bring this matter up on Monday -that is what the press said-I got in touch with the hon. member for Peel and had him here. Every opportunity was given at that time for making any statement which the opposition wished to make-I am not referring now to the hon. member for Kootenay West and his associates. It was known the hon. member for Peel would not be here for the ensuing three days and he was here when it

Supply-Transport
was stated in the press that there was going to be some suggestion, insinuation or something of that kind made against him.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
On that point, would the
Prime Minister give the basis for his statement that we were going to bring this matter up on Monday?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Only the reference in the press to the effect that one of the hon. gentlemen opposite was going to bring it up. There was some reference, either in the press or on the radio, indicating that the Leader of the Opposition intended to press this matter. Immediately I communicated with the hon. member for Peel. The hon. gentlemen first raised this matter last Friday. I noticed then that there were innuendos and implications made, and that the question was likely to be raised again. The hon. member for Peel was here on Monday, available to answer any questions. He was here in the house. From then on he intended to be absent for the next two or three days, and all I can say is this: up to the present, there has been nothing other than these suggestions and inferences and innuendos for which the Leader of the Opposition is not prepared to take responsibility. He realizes that if he goes farther than he does in his suggestions, the fullest opportunity will be given to him to establish any alleged wrongdoing. There has been no suggestion yet of that because from the very beginning he said there was none.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Perhaps we can finish off this question of procedure. I should like to tell the Prime Minister that I am willing to take responsibility for every statement that I have made on this matter, and there is no basis for any statement on his part that I am running away from that responsibility, as he will find out when we get the information. Then the Prime Minister had the effrontry to suggest that because it was stated somewhere in a newspaper that we might be bringing this matter up on Monday he instructed the member for Peel to be here on Monday.
As the Prime Minister knows perfectly well, and if he does not I will refresh his memory, on Friday I first raised this matter and the Prime Minister said he would make a statement later. On Monday he made a statement, and I said at that time we would examine that statement and decide what course we should take. There was no opportunity to deal with this matter until the estimates of the department came up. That would be the first opportunity. The Prime Minister knows himself that the estimates of the Department of Transport could not

come up before Wednesday, so his excuse for the hon. member for Peel not being here is a very feeble one indeed.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Let us be clear. The
way in which this has been done in the past when this-I will not call it McCarthyism- has been indulged in is to face the issue. At any time the hon. gentleman can make the necessary motion, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier once said. I hope he will take that course, because on the face of the facts he will realize he can go no further than make suggestions-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
I know something about
McCarthyism, and I say to the Prime Minister that McCarthyism means when a man is charged before you know the facts.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
That is what you are
doing.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
When we get the facts we
will decide what action should be taken. Does the Prime Minister say that that is McCarthyism? Let me remind him of some of the things he used to do over here when he was attacking the government without a complete basis of information. His suggestion that our effort to get the facts from the minister is McCarthyism is not worthy of him.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I will not enter into that discussion. I will simply say that the Leader of the Opposition has followed a course of innuendo but is fearful lest he go beyond that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I deprecate the statement which the Prime Minister has just made to the effect that the Leader of the Opposition has followed a course of innuendo rather than proceed in the manner in which the Prime Minister indicated on the orders of the day, I believe on Monday. The Prime Minister is too good a lawyer not to know that this is not the only method by which a matter of this kind can be proceeded with. The Prime Minister has been in the house far too long-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
What would be that other
method?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I will come to it in a moment. The Prime Minister has been in the house far too long to try to throw the burden over to this side of the house and to attempt to scare the opposition into not pursuing this matter.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: He has encouraged it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
That is exactly what the Prime Minister tried to do the other evening. If he is encouraging it, why does he not allow us to debate this matter as it should be debated, not by seeking information and

asking questions and prying it out, as we have to do. The position is this: the Prime Minister hastened, on the orders of the day, to say that the opposition would be given all the opportunities they wanted. Let them debate it all they like, he said. Let them have no complaint about the government. We are complaining now about the manner in which this question is being handled, and I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is so courageous he should give us an opportunity to consider this matter fully. Why does he not have the hon. member for Peel make a statement so that we may know exactly what the facts are.
I said a moment ago that I would remind the Prime Minister of another occasion. Does the Prime Minister remember an occasion on which the leader of the opposition in this house charged the Right Hon. C. D. Howe with certain interests having to do with the C. D. Howe Company? Does he remember that was a clear cut charge in express language or in any way you might put it? It was debated in this house day in and day out by innuendo and in every other way. It was talked of outside the house and it was talked of here. Was the leader of the opposition asked to resign because he was not able to substantiate his charge? Of course he was not. Surely this is not a new procedure. Surely because no charge is laid against an hon. member is no reason to deny information to those of us who want that information? I am sure the Prime Minister, he who has been speaking about introducing a bill of rights, would be the last one to do so. That is one of the foremost things concerning a bill of rights, that we should be entitled to information. Well, let us have that information.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: What information do you want that you have not been given? You have had every question answered, and every piece of material has been given to you.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: My friend gets exercised a bit-

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I just want you to answer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: It is not for me to answer, but you.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: I will answer any question you ask, except to comment on the judgment of the court, because I will abide by the judgment of the court.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Order. I would ask hon. members to please address their questions through the Chair. I would also remind hon. members that the hon. member for Kootenay West was on his feet and making a speech, which I allowed

hon. members to interrupt to deal with a specific point about the role of the hon. member for Peel. If they have concluded their remarks on that particular matter I would ask the hon. member for Kootenay West to continue with his remarks.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I make one short comment and then I will resume my seat; I am sure there will be no objection to it. The judgment of the court is a clear cut condemnation of the member for Peel.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to express my sincere appreciation for the hon. members exhibiting the tolerance which permits me to continue with the speech I started some minutes ago. We have listened very carefully to this debate and I can truthfully say that the hon. members of this group want to be as fair as possible on this issue. It is very easy to get worked up on one side or the other.
I said in my preceding remarks that we had hoped that the hon. member for Peel would have been in his seat. We think it would have been more appropriate on this occasion, but the Prime Minister has apparently explained that. We have listened to the questions asked by the Leader of the Opposition and other very important people in the front benches of the official opposition and to the answers given by the Minister of Transport. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I could not sleep last night again. I am a very bad sleeper on occasions. However, I read an article in Maclean's magazine about the Minister of Transport.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext: Not that.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
It mentioned his ability as a cadet and as a boxer. I was a boxer on one occasion and got knocked out on the same occasion. I was also a soldier and I would pay tribute to his record overseas, and as a political organizer and businessman. I do think this afternoon that he has exhibited a certain amount of ability to lay down what I would call a good smoke screen, and I do not think he has answered these questions directly enough. We in this group think it is most unfair for this issue to be left up in the air. It is most unfair to the member concerned and to the house. From what I can judge from listening very carefully, there are serious contradictions between statements made by the hon. member for Peel outside of this house and statements given to this house by the minister. I think that is accepted by everybody. There are very serious discrepancies between the statements made by

the hon. member for Peel outside the house and the statements made by the evaluator before the exchequer court. If statements made by a person giving evidence before the exchequer court are not correct, then that person has committed perjury.
To indicate how this type of situation creates doubt, confusion and suspicion, unfairly to the member for Peel and unfairly in the general approach of this house to this question our group received yesterday and today phone calls from various parts, and also letters in today's mail. These clearly indicate that it is a question which the public of this country would like to see cleared up. There is confusion, there is doubt and there is concern. I will be quite frank, Mr. Chairman, and say after listening to the questions and answers, in my opinion the hon. member for Peel exercised what I would call immature and poor judgment. That would be my opinion. But I think in fairness to him the whole matter should be cleared up, and on that account this group would support the request of the official opposition that a committee be appointed to inquire into the whole	matter	to settle it	once	and for all.The	Acting	Chairman	(Mr.	McCleave):
Shall the resolution carry?

speechtext:

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to say anything about this matter of Malton valuations at all until the Prime Minister made his intervention this afternoon. I could not help but feel that one point had not been made by anyone and that it seems to me is the most obvious of all. In his judgment the president of the exchequer court has made statements about a member of this house which certainly call into question-and I am not calling it into question; it was the president of the exchequer court who did it-the propriety of his conduct as a member of this house.
I would not have thought it would have required the Leader of the Opposition or the humblest member of this committee to bring up this matter. I would have thought that the hon. member for Peel himself as was his right and, I suggest, his duty, under our rules, would have taken the first opportunity to give this committee the explanation to which it is entitled and which it has not received. I do not intend to say anything more about the hon. member's conduct when he is not here; but I do want to say a word or two about the conduct of the Minister of Transport and I wish to make these comments in a very non-controversial way because I as a minister was faced with a precisely similar situation to the one with which the minister was faced.
I was faced with expropriations which were being made by the organization over which my friend the hon. member for Laurier provided in his capacity as president of the St. Lawrence seaway. I was acting as a trustee for the persons who were being expropriated in the Caughnawaga Indian reserve. A very high proportion of those cases had been settled. Proposals were made to me, not by a member of parliament it is true, but proposals similar to those made to

the Minister of Transport when he first came into office, that the department should try to deal in a different way with the group of dissenters from the way in which the majority of those who had assented had been treated. I said that was an impossible course for the government to take and that the vast majority of these people having accepted, on a certain basis, the government could not subsequently give better treatment to others, and ever face the public.
I therefore think the minister was wrong to appoint this special evaluator. In my opinion, based on such experience as I have had, he should have told the hon. member for Peel that he could not entertain this proposal, that the settlements had been made with all these other people in comparable circumstances and that those who were not satisfied had their recourse to the courts and that that was the place for the cases to be settled.
The Chairman presiding over this debate prior to your taking the chair, Mr. Chairman, raised the question as to whether this matter was relevant. It seems to me it is entirely relevant. One hundred and eighty of these cases having been settled on a certain basis it would, in my view, have been the height of inequity for the government of its own motion to give better treatment to the remaining twelve. Those people could take the matter before the courts and try to get better treatment as one ultimately did, but that is another matter.
I am not criticizing the minister very strongly for this because I realize that, in 1957, he was new, inexperienced and eager, but I do say that I think the minister was guilty in this particular instance of a very serious error of judgment.

(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, according to the documents given to me by the Minister of Transport, on June 9, 1958 he received from Mr. Robert Sauve, of St. Johns, a request to the effect that Messrs. Robert and Bernard Goineau should be allowed to set up gas pumps and a workshop for yacht repairs on the federal site I mentioned.
Mr. Chairman, I want to call the attention of the minister to that matter. I have

no wish to condemn his attitude, but I want to warn him of the existing situation before the lease is signed. If a lease has been offered, before the minister decides what he proposes to do, I want to warn him that the population of St. Johns will not view with favour the fact that the department or the Minister of Transport is giving a piece of public property to private citizens.
If the government disposed of a great stretch of land in that sector on the banks of the Richelieu river, we might perhaps consider such request to dispose of public property, but at this time, that site is the only one in the town of St. Johns, which gives access to the ships, boats and yachts, so that if use of that public site were alienated it would mean a discrimination against the people of my riding and my city.
Mr. Chairman, may I recall the steps that have been taken-and I want to be clearly understood: the Conservative candidate, Mr. Robert Sauve, asked the minister on June 9, 1958, to give Messrs. Robert and Bernard Goineau the opportunity of operating gas stations and a repair shop on a public site. Moreover, the mayor of the town of St. Johns, who is a friend of the defeated candidate, wrote to the minister on August 25, 1958, telling him that he had been told of such request having been made in favour of Messrs. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on tolls on the Welland ship canal. I have spoken in the house several times against the imposition of tolls on this canal because I have said it would toll-lock lake Ontario.
The greatest percentage of the industry in Ontario making use of the water-borne traffic is situated around the shores of lake Ontario and along the Welland ship canal. Areas around the shores of lake Ontario are the source of very little raw material, so that most of the raw material has to be brought in through a toll area. In today's Globe and Mail there is an article by Mr. Forgie of the Ontario Paper Company, Thorold, an outstanding economist, and he urges that the Canadian people recognize the importance of the great lakes waterway system. He predicts that otherwise the development of Canada as a trading nation through the advantage of having the seaway can be strangled by the broad application of policies which have not been fitted to serve local and particular needs. He notes that Premier Frost has come out

Supply-Transport
against the imposition of tolls on the canal. With reference to the particular position of the Ontario Paper Company at Thorold he says:
We have built docking facilities to load newsprint, pulp and pulpwood and have built up a fleet of ten ships which transport our raw materials and finished products throughout the great lakes system. We gain no benefit from improved depth facilities on the canal, yet we cannot move a ton of paper or a stick of pulpwood without paying a toll on a facility which has been completely paid for through taxes.
I realize, however, that the Welland canal tolls are just being charged for the cost of the deepening. The article continues:
He said the principle of tolls had been introduced in such a way that a Canadian ship leaving a lake Ontario port is no longer able to proceed freely through the great lakes system.
I might say that the shippers along the canal are at a very great disadvantage now. It is costing them more to bring in pulpwood. It is costing the Steel Company of Hamilton more to bring in iron ore and their ships cannot make as many trips per season as they did in previous years. There is a lot of talk- we have heard it in parliament-about enlarging the Welland ship canal or duplicating a certain number of locks. I think this is particularly bad for our area because the manufacturers in the area think that it will add to the cost of shipping in future years. Also, the plants that are there will not expand because they are afraid of higher shipping costs.
The minister said a few minutes ago that only members of his party speak for the small people. I am trying to speak now for the small people in our area, the men who want to keep their jobs. The Hon. Charles Daley, minister of labour of Ontario, has made many pronouncements against tolls on the Welland ship canal and I know that Premier Frost came out again tolls about a month before they were imposed. According to the press two or three weeks ago, at the time of the christening of a new ship at Port Weller, Mr. Daley and others made protests in the presence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and according to the press and some people who were there the minister, after listening to the protests, said that he would take up the matter with the cabinet in Ottawa.
I asked him in the house if any protest had been made and his answer was in the negative. I do not know whether or not I worded my question properly. He may have thought that I was asking whether any written protest had been made. But in the presence of a good many people who were present that day protests were certainly made to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and he said they would be taken up with the cabinet

in Ottawa. I should like to ask the minister today if he has been receiving further protests from people about tolls on the Welland canal and if the Minister of Trade and Commerce has conveyed the protests made on that day to the members of the cabinet.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday on this item I referred to the St. Lawrence seaway and to what in my opinion are some very important faults in the construction of the seaway and made certain statements resulting from my own personal observations. I asked the minister at that time to consider referring the whole question of the seaway to a standing committee of the house for discussion and examination. I felt that this was necessary not only because of the apparent serious construction faults but also because of answers given to questions asked in the house as to the movement of piers, steps taken to bring about repairs to piers, remedial measures as they were termed, and the very startling revelation in my judgment that the piers of the Cornwall bridge do not go down to bedrock. I take it that the minister is refusing an inquiry by such a committee. I think he is making a very serious mistake.
Almost daily we see further evidence of difficulties of all kinds in the operation of the seaway and this suggests to me that not only with respect to construction but also to operation there are a great many things that require the most thorough and serious examination. There is a report today that it is impossible now for the dominion bureau of statistics to obtain accurate reports of tonnage going through the seaway. I have in my hand an article by Clark Davey in this morning's Globe and Mail which reads in part as follows:
A change in method of reporting ship movements and cargo statistics has left the dominion bureau of statistics without any accurate records for the first weeks of St. Lawrence seaway operations. The seaway authority is expected to issue its own report shortly on the number of ships and total cargoes handled to the end of May.
However, D.B.S. officials said they have been unable to obtain an accurate break-down of commodity figures essential to economic studies of the seaway's impact and of changing traffic patterns.
The article goes on to say that D.B.S. officials have endeavoured to find out the quantity of goods going through the seaway but that the clerks have all been moved to

the seaway office in Cornwall where they receive the forms from the ship owners or agents. The article continues:
The clerks, in turn, transmit the information to the dominion bureau of statistics. In many cases, D.B.S. officials said, the ship owners or agents are simply not filling in the forms. In many other cases the information they provide is incomplete or wrong. They said repeated checks would have to be made and it would be several months, they expected, before the system was operating satisfactorily.
This may not sound too important to the minister but I think it is important that accurate statistics be readily available as to the traffic through the seaway. Surely if we are to know the value of the seaway it is absolutely essential that such statistics be readily available. This is another instance of inefficient operation. As stated by the dominion bureau of statistics, because of the lack of information it is impossible to report accurately the amount of traffic going through the seaway.
I related to the committee yesterday what I had seen so far as the locks near Montreal are concerned, and what I believe to be very serious errors in construction. I had asked why the piers did not go down to bedrock. I see no explanation from the minister as to why the peirs did not go down to bedrock. I see no statement by the minister which would suggest that the piers should not have gone down to bedrock.
The minister quotes from information with which he has been supplied to the effect that certain remedial measures were taken. He said that a preliminary report dated January 11, 1958 included the statement that the remedial measures being taken are reasonable ones.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
I am now going to make the speech I have always intended making on the estimates of the Department of Transport and I assure the minister that I am going to be speaking for the little people of Newfoundland as indeed I have tried to do on many other subjects besides the minister's estimates in seeking to further the interests of the fishermen, though I have not been able to do much to soften the hard hearts of members of the government in this respect. But the heart of the Minister of Transport is, perhaps, softer than those of his colleagues and I want to start by supporting very warmly the appeal made to the minister yesterday by the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador and the plea I made on behalf of that hon. member a year ago when he was not able to be in the house. The hon. member stated the problem, but I should like to say something about the background to this problem.
At the time the terms of union were negotiated ten years ago it was decided by the then government that the telegraph and telephone service formerly operated by the department of posts and telegraphs of Newfoundland would be taken over by Canadian National Telegraphs but because, for certain historical reasons, telecommunications in Labrador had not been under the administration of the posts and telegraphs of Newfoundland no similar action was taken in that area. Labrador is an integral part of the province of Newfoundland and it does seem to me that the people of Labrador-I am sorry to say I do not represent them though I would love to; they are represented very adequately by my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador-deserve an improved service. I would remind the minister,

as I may say I reminded some of his predecessors-I say this in the presence of one of them today-that the large centres are better served. The minister smiles and I know that he thinks he is doing a lot better than previous ministers. This is one respect in which he can show his interest in the small people about whom he was speaking. I hope he will get up and tell us that it is the intention of the government to reorganize these communications or, alternatively, entrust the whole problem to the C.N.T. As a matter of fact, I think the second course would be better than the first. I can understand that the minister should not want bureaucrats to be running a telegraph service, if I may use the minister's word, but I think the C.N.T. is much better equipped. And I should like to add that despite occasional criticisms that are heard in Newfoundland-and I may be taken to task by some of my constituents for saying this-I think the Canadian National Telegraphs has done a marvellous job in Newfoundland in the last ten years. I think it is really remarkable the way they have increased the efficiency of the service and modernized it under very difficult conditions, and I am informed that they have been somewhat surprised to find that when they had modernized their equipment and improved the service the financial position was improved instead of the reverse.
I would suggest to the minister that no matter how much recovery is made this year, we are going to have seasonal unemployment again next winter in Newfoundland, and if any way can be found to have advanced planning, perhaps on a larger scale, for the modernization of the telephone and telegraph system in order to provide employment, it would be welcome. I know you cannot cut the poles in winter but you can put them up. After all the minister does have to take the over-all financial responsibility for the budget of the C.N.T. even if it is not a direct responsibility, and I think this is another way in which he could help very constructively.
I also want to say a brief word about something which I would not have mentioned today but for one thing, namely, the absence of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador from the city today. I refer to the question of the port of Botwood and the pilotage there. I do feel that this situation at Botwood is a very special one. It is important to keep this port open for the longest period of the year in order to maximize the returns of the pulp and paper industry and to enable them to keep the maximum number of men in employment. There are some special difficulties which I will not discuss now, but I say that I have
Supply-Transport
always found the department exceedingly co-operative in these matters. I know I can say the same for my colleague, the hon. member for that district.
While I am still dealing with the problems of my hon. friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador I do not think he would mind if I also endorsed what he had to say about the hotel at Gander. Gander, after all, is only five miles and a few moose away from my constituency, and it is a place to which I generally go when I am going to my constituency. It is a place in which I have taken a great interest and a place in which the taxpayers of Canada have invested tens of millions and, no doubt, hundreds of millions of dollars. And it is in our view the most important airport in Canada if not in the world.
There is a real danger that unless a little more energy and initiative is put into getting a hotel there as near as possible to the terminal there will be increased pressure on the part of the international air lines to avoid Gander whenever they can, and this very big investment may be lost because of a relatively small matter. I know the department does not want to run a hotel, and I do not blame them, but I think that rather than jeopardize the whole investment in Gander they should consider even that. However, I think there are other ways in which the problem could be taken care of.
I should like the minister to tell us, if he can, and if there is anything to tell, just what it is we read in a mysterious way about the free port on the south coast of Newfoundland. We keep reading items in the papers and see it suggested from time to time that the members from Newfoundland are neglecting their duties because they are not supporting this project which we are told the Minister of Transport is terribly eager to advance. I think the public in Newfoundland would like to know. Certainly I would like to know, and I am sure my friend from St. John's East would also like to know what the score really is, if there is any score.
So as not to leave out any canal in the country I am not going to ask the minister about the canal across the Avalon peninsula, which would shorten the journey to Europe appreciably. The minister can put that down for his long term planning.

Not to my knowledge, Mr. Chairman. Then the hon. member mentioned the Newfoundland railway and changes in the gauge of the Newfoundland railway, but I have had no report on that recently from the Canadian National.
Next he mentioned the Chignecto canal, and I would like to read a report made for me on that matter. This was submitted by the economics division of the Department of Transport and it reads as follows:
Estimates of cost have risen greatly since the surveyor commission estimated in 1931 the cost of a smaller project than now being studied at $48 million. The estimates now run from $90 million to $140 million. An alternative plan has been submitted by the Foundation Engineering Company and this too has been referred to engineers for study. The question of hydroelectric power development in connection with a canal has been given consideration, and thus far it would appear that engineering opinion is generally agreed that the two projects could be treated independently; in other words there would be no substantial savings from a joint project.
At the same time the department has undertaken to obtain information on the possible economic value of a Chignecto canal. In view of the comparatively heavy cost of construction this is an important aspect of the question but not one on which it is easy to reach definite conclusions. We know of certain items of traffic that might use a Chignecto canal but whether the canal is capable of attracting sufficient long distance traffic from present routes to justify its construction is still problematical.
Both the engineering and economic studies are continuing and reports should be received some time this summer.

speechtext: I wonder if the minister could say who was doing the engineering study and who was doing the economic study?

minor way. We have heard a lot in this committee with respect to rail and air transportation and today we heard from one who presumes to speak with authority on water transportation. It is my hope that within the next few months the department will reconsider the entire question of air terminal facilities not only across Canada but will consider along with the hotel at Gander the need for proper landing and takeoff facilities in our smaller western centres. As the

minister is probably aware this is the only major hotel in that part of the province. I believe it is one of the few hotels operated by the C.N.R. that operates at a profit. It is not necessary for me to take the time of the committee to point out the necessity for the provision of these additional facilities because, as I said a moment ago, an excellent case has been made out for this by prominent groups in the city of St. John's and I would ask the minister to take this into consideration.
The second point I would ask to be considered is one with which I dealt with briefly last session during consideration of the minister's estimates. I would suggest that the railway should consider the provision of vital services solely on the basis of need and not on the basis of economics. We realize we are here to try and cut down on the expense of the railway to the extent we can but at the same time as members our primary function is to urge the provision of essential services for those parts of the country where they are badly needed. An express service is vitally needed for Bell island. I would ask the minister if consideration could again be given to this question and if the matter could be re-opened with the Canadian National Railways with a view to providing express service to serve the 13,000 citizens on Bell island.
My third point concerns the provision in the estimates of this department for the construction of a new ferry to service Bell island. Perhaps when we reach this item or after I resume my seat the minister could report on the progress to date of the auto ferry for Bell island and advise when it is expected that this boat will be finished. Mr. Chairman, I do not apologize at this time for bringing up another matter. The only reason I bring it up now is that it concerns at least two if not three of the divisions of the Department of Transport and I feel I should take it up at this time. I refer to the Dorval airport outside of Montreal.
As the minister knows, there is a great deal of dissatisfaction in Montreal at this time about the progress made in connection with the airport. That dissatisfaction has been engendered not only from groups and associations which are particularly interested in the airport but from others as well. I know of no newspaper in Montreal, in either the French or the English language, which has not severely criticized the Department of Transport on the progress made in recent years. I propose to criticize the department on this score, and it may be that the minister will find that I am responsible to some extent for some of this. If he so finds I will accept it; but none the less, the fact is that for the last two years the government has been in office and there has been little or no progress made.
I refer first to an article which appeared in La Presse of Montreal on June 3, 1959, entitled:
Une "strategic sinistre"?
There can be no doubt about the feeling of those who read this article that there is a differentiation in the department between what is happening in Montreal and what is happening elsewhere. I will not go any farther at the moment.
Then there is the very serious complaint that appeared in the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Star and in the statement made by the Montreal tourist and convention bureau. I may tell the minister at once that I was wholly dissatisfied with the answer he gave me on the orders of the day in which he indicated that far more progress had been made under his administration than under the former administration. I have no objection if he wants to say that and repeat it ad infinitum, but that does not derogate from the responsibility which rests on the government to get on with the airport in Montreal.
I am in the airport in Montreal at least once a week and sometimes more often, and I agree with the statement of the Montreal tourist bureau that it is a shame as to what has happened. I know that the position is, well, we will not do anything with the old airport until the new one is ready. That, of course, is a very tempting conclusion to come to and perhaps the natural one in all the circumstances; but if the new airport was

coming along I think people would be able to put up with the difficulties in the old one, but the new airport does not seem to be moving at all. As a matter of fact, it is growing at a snail's pace.
What did the Montreal tourist bureau have to say? I will not deal in personalities; I will deal objectively. They state that the first view given travellers entering the country through the local airport is simply disgusting. Why would the Montreal tourist bureau want to make a statement like that unless there was some foundation for it? There is some foundation for it. All hon. members have to do is to go there and see. Particularly when various flights come in simultaneously, you just cannot get through the general area in the airport building, let alone all the other difficulties that take place. La Presse, in an editorial in the June 3 issue, said this:
(Translation):
Since the actual beginning of the works at Dorval, which was about five years ago-
(Text):
Listen to this carefully because I know the minister understands quite well. (Translation):
-there has been time to start and complete the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, to dot Montreal with skyscrapers, to build a number of airports in other cities, to make improvements to the Toronto airport on two separate occasions and to draw plans for a new air terminal in the Queen city that will likely be ready before that of Montreal. And when the Minister of Transport is questioned about it in parliament, he is satisfied to give a politician's reply and say that the present government is progressing more rapidly than the previous one. Unfortunately, the facts far from confirm such a breezy answer.
(Text):
I may add that I go to Malton airport from time to time and I am delighted with the progress that has been made there. There is a real attempt to expand the airport and divide the various areas so that with a little bit of common sense travellers know where to go quickly and can move to and from the building with dispatch. But why should not that be done in the city of Montreal?
I raise this in conjunction with another matter and I am sure the minister will not blame me if I bring it up. I refer to the air agreements. There are some of us who are beginning to have apprehensions about what is likely to happen to the international airport at Montreal. The minister announced the other day an amendment to the United Kingdom air transport agreement and one of the bargains made in the agreement was that in exchange for certain rights which T.C.A. was to get in the United Kingdom and onward B.O.A.C. would get additional landing rights elsewhere, namely at Toronto.

Nobody is going to find fault with this but what I do become apprehensive about is that in the Financial Post of June 6, 1959 there is a statement to the effect that six transAtlantic carriers now landing at Montreal are seeking similar rights to go on to Toronto. If this is going to be the case, if the minister, the department and the government in their negotiation of air agreements make the situation such that the importance of Montreal from an air standpoint is going to be far less than it has been in the past, then I think that is a serious matter. I do not charge the minister with anything personal in this regard. I know that he has in mind the general development of aviation in Canada, as have his officers. On the oher hand, I do know that when you start negotiating across the table for changes in an air agreement you have to bargain here and bargain there. Where you give in here you must get something elsewhere, and if in the bargaining it is Dorval airport that is going to be left holding the bag then I am afraid that the situation will certainly be a serious one.
I protest as strongly as I can about the delays at the Montreal airport. I am not the only one protesting. Anyone who knows what is going on is doing the same thing. The press is very apprehensive about the matter and so are those people who are air minded. So are the air lines which have to rely on facilities in order to move travellers from one airport to another with dispatch and efficiency. I should like to get some information about the airport and ask the minister a few questions. Yes, I am glad to be able to say we feel confident the airport will be ready for operation next year. I am glad to assure the hon. member that the work is going ahead. As he has said, there has been a temporary slowdown lately and this was caused by certain holdups at treasury board. They have all been overcome and the contracts have been passed. The work is going ahead.
I might give some information on the details. The terminal building itself is in an advanced state, with the office floors and the basement virtually completed, the remaining work being related to the finishing off of the public waiting room and airline operating space on the main and mezzanine floors. This work is now proceeding. In addition, there remains completion of the main power plant installation in the building, the construction of the fingers and aeroquays, the installation of the hydrant refuelling system, the construction of the new main heating plant which will serve the building and the whole airport, and the paving of the apron in front of the building. The first stage of tender calls in connection with hydrant refuelling work and the heating plant is under way, and the final stage of tender calls will go out shortly. The plans for the fingers and aeroquays are at present being modified. Initial plans for this purpose, while satisfactory in concept, had to be studied in detail from the point of view of cost of construction in relation to the overall cost and revenue position of the terminal as a whole. It was found that the cost of the structures would be rather high and would make it difficult to maintain our objective of self-sufficiency of operation and decision was taken, without varying the concept, to try to modify the plans as regards construction costs. This planning should be completed during the summer, so that construction work may commence thereafter in time to permit the opening of the building, as I previously stated, sometime next year.
With regard to the new air agreement giving B.O.A.C. the right to go into Malton, I might say that we did not seek to enter into any new air agreement with the British. We have been under considerable pressure, ever since I came into office over the past two years, to do so. Talks finally took place just last spring and, as I say, we were under great pressure. I think the minister understands these matters very well. It would have been impossible for us not to conclude the agreement which he has mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, since I have heard the hon. member for Richelieu-Verche-res inviting the Prime Minister to visit the Richelieu river in connection with the canalization of the Richelieu river, I would like to state here that I have already invited the Prime Minister to visit the Chambly canal and I expect a favourable answer. I would also like to invite the Minister of Transport to visit the Chambly canal. He would then be greeted royally and entertained as only the people of my riding can entertain.
Speaking of the Richelieu canal, I would like to refer the hon. Minister of Transport to the brief from the city of Sorel to the federal government for the modernization of the Richelieu-Champlain canal presented by a delegation presided over by Dr. Robert Fiset, mayor of Sorel, accompanied by many mayors from communities along the Richelieu banks in my constituency. This brief was supported by a delegation consisting of representatives of a number of United States and Canadian chambers of commerce, municipalities, service clubs and other interested groups and all of which are situated in the area to be served by the proposed improved Richelieu-Champlain canal. May I mention here a study made by Clayton Sinclair in the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, May 31, 1958,
IThe Acting Chairman (Mr. McGee).]
on page 4 of that issue. Mr. Sinclair gives a fair resume of the situation on the Champlain canal. He says:
Like a cute youngster, the Richelieu canal has never been able to prove to its elders that it's growing up.
Industry is springing up along its shores but the function of the 409-mile water route, linking Canada's St. Lawrence river ports with New York city, is still basically the same as it was when it got its start 113 years ago.
One of the oldest canals in Canada, the Richelieu has stood by while other inland waterways took their turn at modernization.
Now, its boosters think it's about time that some serious thought is given the Richelieu system. In the past, they say, it's been a matter of governments preferring to leave traffic patterns as they were instead of destroying the beauty of the Richelieu setting.
Once, this was sufficient. But now, with industry spreading out from Montreal and above everything else, the development of Quebec's north shore gulf area, the Richelieu's potentialities are challenging.
May I add here that a recent announcement has been made that an important steel plant is being built at Contrecoeur near Sorel. These developments, together with more development either on the Quebec north shore or this part of the south shore from Sorel to Varennes would amply justify the government in undertaking and examining the possibility of developing the Richelieu seaway from Sorel to St. Johns, via the Chambly canal. Speaking of the Chambly canal, may I add a little information which would justify the government in looking to see if it is possible to widen the Chambly canal at the seaway between Chambly and St. Johns.
In the same study by Clayton Sinclair we read:
Chief among these-
That is, those who are using the Richelieu river.
-is the north shore gulf region, where iron ore for Pennsylvania smelters, newsprint for New York printing houses, and aluminum, would originate.
Eastern paper mills produce one million tons of newsprint annually for the New York area, of which only 26,000 tons now move by the short Richelieu route.
Added to this are the huge annual shipments of iron ore from Seven Islands and other ore ports in the gulf.
Closer to home, Sorel, at the mouth of the Richelieu, each year ships 250,000 tons of titanium slag and pure iron to American Atlantic ports.
Mr. Chairman, the Richelieu lies about 43 miles down river from Montreal. It is a quiet river which occasionally floods its banks in the spring, but it is serene for what is the remainder of a seven-month navigation season from the latter days of April to early November. This justifies my contention that we should look forward to the development of this seaway canal along the Richelieu river.
May I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we are on this item of canals, I should like to refer the minister to a project of considerable interest and importance to the residents of the city of Ottawa and also of the Ottawa

valley generally. I refer to the project to make the city of Ottawa an ocean port. I believe that a few weeks ago the minister received a delegation which was representative of a large section of the Ottawa valley and included officials from the city of Ottawa, the city of Hull, the eastern Ontario development association, the federation of chambers of commerce of western Quebec, the county officials of the counties of Pontiac and Renfrew, officials of the Ottawa river development association and many others.
I know that this project is linked with a far larger project in magnitude, namely the making of the Ottawa river, lake Nipissing and the French river a seaway. In such a case the seaway would be the strong right arm of the present St. Lawrence seaway. It may not be a project that is ripe at the present time and at this particular moment I do not want to enter into all of the technical aspects of the question. Suffice it to tell the committee that this matter has been explored and looked into by engineers of the Department of Transport and also by other competent authorities since as far back as 1885. Even at that time, without the technical means at their disposal that we have today, it was found that the project was certainly feasible and possible.
What prompts me to bring this matter to the attention of the committee at the present time is that the province of Quebec at the present time is contemplating harnessing the rapids at Carillon. The province of Quebec expects to spend a sum perhaps as high as $200 million on that project within the next few years. There are locks at Carillon but they have a draft of only about 8J feet. They will have to be replaced, and if they are to be replaced I submit that the department should investigate seriously the possibility of replacing them with a draft of sufficient depth to accommodate commercial navigation and also deep-sea navigation. By so doing there will be a direct connecting link between the capital city and the present seaway, and that would certainly add greatly to the advantage of the industrial development of the Ottawa valley and would also accommodate industries which exist today.
I refer to one case especially, namely the Hilton mines, which at the present time are shipping iron ore by railway to Toronto and to parts of the United States. With the deepening of the Ottawa river channel from Ottawa to Montreal the ore could be shipped by water, thereby effecting a considerable saving and bringing about other advantages. That is the reason why the numerous associations I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks interviewed the minister a few weeks ago. They think the time is now ripe

to take the first step, the relatively simple Step, of deepening the Ottawa channel for a distance of 119 miles. It is estimated that the cost will amount to between $15 million and $20 million. The first step that can be recommended now is the replacement of the locks at the Carillon dam.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister look into the possibility of appointing some engineers to investigate this matter and to report to him, and he in turn could report to the committee and to the house. I think in so doing we shall be taking the first step toward the improved development of the Ottawa valley and indeed of the entire country because, as appears now, in a few years the present St. Lawrence seaway facilities may become inadequate. If that should happen, the ultimate route would normally be the Ottawa river, lake Nipissing and the French river which, after all, were the first water courses over which the pioneers and the developers of this country passed, and which were in days gone by the great navigational streams of our country. By looking forward in such a way we shall be planning in a logical way for the future development of our country.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The pattern that we have followed in icebreaking between Quebec and Montreal is related primarily to the prevention of flood dangers in the Montreal area and helping local river ports. As I indicated, the river from lake St. Peter to Montreal does not remain open unless the icebreaker fleet is capable of keeping the channel open. It has been normal for us to use three icebreakers from Quebec up to maintain a position from which the channel could be opened in time to prevent serious flooding that could otherwise occur.

speechtext:
I should just like to make a few brief remarks on this item on aids to navigation because they are of growing importance in the constituency which I represent. I am referring particularly to the Columbia river, the upper and lower Arrow lakes, the Kootenay river, Kootenay lake and Slocan lake because of the considerable increase in the number of tugs and the increase in the number of small water craft, particularly those coming up the Columbia river from the United States. As I have said before this session, some may come from as far south as Portland being portaged around the dams in the United States south of the international border. Some come down the Kootenay river into Kootenay lake. Some come in by road from the various ports and then are launched at suitable launching places and other points on the Kootenay lake or on the river or on the Columbia river or the upper and lower Arrow lakes and Slocan lake.
There is an increasing need for better marking, and provision of more marking, particularly with respect to lights in the rivers and buoys and in some cases markers. I want to
Supply-Transport
say that the people of the districts are pleased, particularly those interested in boating, that the department has marked the river between Castlegar and the international boundary. It was a most dangerous part of the river to leave unmarked. There were many craft coming up the river without much knowledge of the channel, the hazards and so on. They appreciate that improvement.
However I want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that it is necessary to have river marking between Arrowhead and Revel-stoke. I might say the same applies to the marking of isolated rocks and things of that sort on the lakes. The local people locate these hazards and sand bars and so on and then press the department to do it. I think that is largely occasioned by the fact that the department uses employees of the Department of Public Works as agents and they are extremely busy indeed.
This matter of the marking of these lakes and rivers and looking after the lights is becoming increasingly important and requires constant attention. As I have said, I think it was five years ago I went down the Columbia and one of the captains told me there were 11 buoys out, a most dangerous situation. I was told they had been out for three months and there was nobody to replace them because the person who was paid to do it never went near the place. That was just because the persons who supervise this work are too busy with other work to check frequently. I am of the opinion that, particularly with respect to the southern interior lakes, possibly the time is coming when somebody should be especially appointed to have jurisdiction over aids to navigation. I think of high water on the Columbia, when a good many of these buoys are washed out. No one notices it for two or three months. A tug comes along or particularly a small craft from the United States, and the first thing you know it is on a sand bar. I think it might be in the interests of the public generally as well as for better administration if someone were given particular charge of watching these buoys, blinker lights and things like that on the interior lakes.
I am not blaming anyone for this situation, as years ago there was just the occasional blinker light or buoy, and so on, because the captains knew the routes. Intensive marking was not required as is required today to make the rivers and lakes safe for watercraft. I do hope consideration will be given to marking the river from Arrowhead to Revelstoke. For instance, last year about 85 small craft came up from the United States and 12 of them went to Revelstoke. I see them all if I am at home because they pass my ranch and many come in to see me. But out of the 12 which
