Mr. Chairman, I presume that this is the vote under which we could ask
the Minister of Transport a most important question and that is is he now in a position to express his views or those of the government on the establishment of a coastguard service for Canada? I ask that question because I and so many others well remember the long and oft repeated demands of the Conservatives when they sat on this side of the chamber to the effect that the government should undertake the establishment of a coastguard service in Canada. We would all like to know whether the Conservatives in changing sides have changed their position with regard to the establishment of a coastguard service. What are the views of the minister on this matter?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman first of all I think we must not be hypnotized by the word "coastguard". That is the word used to describe the service provided in the United States. Here in Canada although we have not such an ear-catching word the same kind of service is provided by various government departments. The Department of National Defence provides search and rescue service. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police provide coastal patrol. The Department of Transport, the Department of Fisheries and the navy provide ships which undertake sea rescue. With these various services combining, we believe the same service is provided as is provided by the United States coastguard.
There are very few services of any kind that cannot be improved, and I have been giving this matter considerable thought during the past few weeks and so has my colleague, the Minister of National Defence. We are actively studying it at this moment and so are our departments. It seems to me that improvements can be made in better co-ordination of the services and specialized training and equipment of those who will be actually performing the sea rescue task. I can assure the hon. member, and all the hon. members, that this matter is being very seriously studied right at this moment. During the next few weeks we hope to work out something that will be an improvement over the services that have been provided in the past, although I think those services have been pretty good. But, as I say, there are no services that cannot be improved, and we intend to improve this service just as much as we possibly can.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE

I must say-I cannot help saying it-that the tune has changed in a period of three years because the answer we have just been given by the minister was the self-same answer we received from the Liberals to which the Conservatives in opposition objected so strenuously and so much.

However, we certainly welcome the fact that the minister has such a great interest in it and that there will be improvements, as all the things he told us about just now were identical with those things we were told by the previous minister of a different party.
Can there be a speed-up in the matter of complete co-ordination of all services so that we do not have ever again the situation which developed only recently in the harbour of Vancouver where a ship caught fire after an explosion, sent out an S.O.S. and it was an hour and a half before any assistance got there. It is quite obvious that some arrangements must be made so that a situation of that kind cannot occur again.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE

maintopic: REQUEST FOR HOUSE OF COMMONS SOFTBALL TEAM SCHEDULE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems a little odd to me that, with the amount of shipping on the Atlantic coast, an organization that could have a salvage vessel would find it necessary to receive a subsidy when equivalent equipment on the west coast, although it could do with a subsidy, does not receive one. We have had some of those anomalies before between the east and west coasts. The fact remains, Mr. Chairman- and it is a very serious fact-that Canada is a maritime nation, and all maritime nations should make it a first principle that their shores have some type of protection for vessels coming to those shores, and goodness knows we want them to come, we want their trade.
Mention has been made of air-sea rescue. While that has been very effective in regard to what I would term small rescues, an airman down and perhaps floating around in a rubber boat, or some fishermen floating around in a dory, it is absolutely a joke when it comes to a big ocean-going vessel in distress, it can do nothing whatsoever. It
Supply-Transport
is true an aircraft can spot a vessel and can hover over it and can send out messages, but there is no equipment at all unless reliance is placed upon commercial organizations that have the equipment and are willing to take virtually a gamble. Our shores are protected in that way, and yet year after year they may lose money on those vessels. It is not good enough, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that on the Atlantic coast there should be a subsidy paid for this purpose and not a subsidy paid on the west coast.
I would like to give an instance that occurred within the last while. Quite a sizable vessel got into difficulty off Carmanagh point which is adjacent to the area we term the graveyard of the Pacific where there have been a great many wrecks. This ship called air-sea rescue and an aircraft from Comox air base spotted her position and hovered around. All it could do was to call up the United States coastguard at Neah bay in the state of Washington and ask them to do what they could. The United States coastguard sent a cutter over and there were very high seas running. She got a line on to Malina-that is the name of the vessel-and got all the men off except two. They were then so close in to the rocky shore, and the combers were so huge that the United States coastguard cutter could not stand by any longer and got out; she had not enough power. What did she do? There was no Canadian government agency; no navy equipment or anything to call, so she called up the Island Tug and Barge Company of Victoria and asked them to send out their big tug Sudbury, and the Sudbury went out. She is a huge, powerful salvage tug. She was able to stand in close enough. She got a line aboard and saved the lives of the two men who were there. The next day the Sudbury pulled off the grounded ship and brought her to Victoria where she was repaired.
There is the situation. We are a maritime nation. These big vessels sometimes get into difficulty, and on the Pacific coast we have absolutely nothing to rely upon but these commercial concerns, which, as I say, are taking a gamble. They may make money one year and lose money for three years.
I am not a believer in a coastguard service; I think it is a lot of rot. The United States coastguard service is a misnomer. They deal in all kinds of things, smuggling and fisheries protection. We do not need that kind of thing. We do know, however, that Canada must have its own salvage vessels stationed at crucial points on our coasts or else the government of Canada should be willing to subsidize. speechtext: As the minister knows, the question of pilotage is, of course, one that is extremely important. Dear John:
I have now obtained further information on the veterans' properties near Malton which have been expropriated. You are, of course, more familiar with these cases than I, but I find that the main complaints are:
(1)	Delay in approaching land owners after expropriation;
(2)	Opinion of the land owners that departmental offers are inadequate;
(3)	Loss by the land owners of the "conditional grants" under the Veterans' Land Act.
There certainly were some delays in approaching land owners after expropriation in 1954. Our small real estate staff in Toronto had a great number of cases to deal in Ontario with during that period and fell behind in their approaches to many people because the volume of work was too great. As regards the second complaint that our offers are not high enough, we not only had appraisals made by our own staff, but we employed an independent appraiser with particular reference to the Hatton test case which is now before the exchequer court, and we consulted fully with officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs who concurred in the view that our offers were fair and reasonable.
It is, of course, by no means abnormal to find a wide gap between an offer which we consider fair and reasonable and the value which may be placed upon property by the land owner. Where a gap is too great it is usually desirable to allow the matter to be settled by the court, and frequently one test case in an area gives the basis for direct settlement of others without court intervention.
As for the conditional grants, after reviewing the facts I do not see how we could take account of this in our offers. This conclusion has been reached after full consultation with the Department of Veterans Affairs, which I understand is in agreement with our view. The conditional grant is an extra credit which may be earned by the veteran if he stays in continuous residence for 10 years, but is related to other benefits which he gives up when he obtains this and which are reestablished if he loses the conditional grant.
In order to qualify for the conditional grant, I understand that the veteran must surrender his right to a re-establishment credit which is part of the war gratuity he is entitled to; but if he loses his right to the conditional grant, his right to the re-establishment credit is restored; or, alternatively, if he relocates under the V.L.A. his right to the conditional grant continues without a break. I think you will appreciate from this why we feel that this is a matter which must be handled within the orbit of the Department of Veterans Affairs because of these related factors which exist. This is the strong advice of our real estate and legal officials in consultation with D.V.A.
However, we recognize that this is a complicated matter and it is because of this fact, as well as because of the very high valuation placed upon their property by the veterans themselves, that we thought it would be fair to all concerned if the Hatton case could be settled by the exchequer court and establish a precedent which could be followed in the other settlements. Otherwise the veterans might feel that they had been unfairly treated; or, alternatively, the Department could be accused of being wasteful of the taxpayers' money by giving in to unreasonable demands.
I am anxious to help, and if it is the case that the veterans have retained the services of an independent appraiser and have obtained advice which differs materially from that available to us, we would be glad to arrange a further meeting to discuss the matter with all concerned, including officials of the V.L.A. I would not like to commit myself at this stage to arbitration in the sense of appointing an independent appraiser acceptable to both the veterans and ourselves until after this meeting takes place. However, I would certainly be prepared to consider this possibility further if the veterans were prepared to agree by contract in advance the report of such an independent appraiser was final and binding on them.
Perhaps you would let me have your views as to what further steps might usefully be taken. Meanwhile, since we have some preference for seeing the Hatton case decided as a means of establishing a basis for settlement of the other cases, we will ask the Department of Justice to request the exchequer court to give earnest consideration to setting an early hearing of the Hatton case.
Yours sincerely,
George Hees.

I hate to bother you with such things, but I have had a telephone call and a telegram; Bill Beach has had telephone calls; and apparently Speers, the land agent in Toronto, has made the statement that he-and not the minister-is running the department in Toronto.
I have had a talk with Earl Clare, whom you appointed for the purpose of evaluating small holdings, and he tells me that Speers was in Ottawa today, apparently with some proposal to the deputy minister or assistant deputy minister that Clare be taken off the job.
